links.summary: Subframe is a design tool — drag & drop, layers, inspector — where "the canvas is based on HTML & React, so you can implement it exactly as designed," and it's "a browser, for building": open localhost or any website in built-in browser tabs, iterate live with visual edits, and work with Claude Code and Codex directly in Subframe ("The agent that sees what you see") using your own subscription, or bring design context to external agents via the Subframe MCP. Free is $0/month for one project with unlimited viewers & editors and limited AI credits; Pro is $20/editor/month for unlimited projects and 6x AI credits.

Complexity is never a conscious design goal, but it arises inherently as new features are pursued and new components introduced — and left unchecked, production stacks "become sprawling patchworks combining everything under the sun." The remedy is production minimalism: retire old technology when something new comes in, standardize on as few components as possible, avoid custom software and installed services, and aim at R. Buckminster Fuller's ephemeralization — "Do more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing." "It seems that perfection is reached not when there is nothing left to add, but when there is nothing left to take away."

Tripwire is "the firewall for your OSS projects": install the GitHub App and it triggers workflows from contributor activity — "Keep the good, reject the bad." Composable rules like account age, rate limits, hidden links, and max files changed screen every change request, with org members exempt, runs public and deciding gated, and "One comment. One check. Zero noise." Access is by waitlist — "Request access" or "Join the beta" — with no pricing shown.

Koboyo is an infinite canvas: "Double-click anywhere to add text or pick a tool" — R for rectangle, O for ellipse, A for arrow, or the picker for all tools. It also offers Zoom & reset view, Keyboard shortcuts, and Slides & Diagrams as Code.

dithered charts & components for shadcn/ui — install via @dither-kit/cli, which "pulls core + deps automatically" with a lockfile for update / diff, or paste into Claude Code, Cursor, or any agent to install + wire up a chart, with files landing in components/dither-kit/. Charts are tweaked from the floating dial panel with knobs like variant, bloom, stackType, colors, animate, and interactive — and the standalone button and gradient "don't pull in the chart engine."

HTTP is "the foundation of data exchange on the web" — clients send requests, servers return responses, and intermediaries relay between them — and the page walks through how that works, from methods, URLs, headers and status codes to the stateless design that cookies and tokens patch up. It then traces the versions (0.9 through 3, where QUIC replaces TCP) and the three core building blocks — headers, methods, status codes — before covering security: HTTPS, HSTS, CORS, CSP, session cookies, and challenge-response authentication. A long "See also" list links out to headers, methods, status, HTTPS, caching, CORS, cookies and dozens more.

MotherDuck is "The Cloud Data Warehouse Built on DuckDB" — fast, serverless analytics with "dedicated compute for every user and every agent," where you can "Build a data stack in one prompt, or plug into the one you have." Its agent-first architecture gives every person, dashboard, and agent session its own isolated DuckDB instance (a "Duckling") with cold starts under 100ms — "no noisy neighbors, no queues, no warehouse-wide slowdowns" — plus Flights for Python pipelines, Guides as "the context layer for agents," and Dives for agent-built visualizations. Interfaces include MCP, CLI, and REST, and it works with the tools you know, from Hex, dbt, Fivetran, Tableau, and Airflow to Python, Java, and C++.",

celld is a self-hosted Durable Objects runtime: Workers handle requests, while Durable Objects, KV, Queues, D1, and Workflows keep their state in cells, each with its own SQLite database, and nodes share a bucket for durable storage. It’s for people who want control over where cells run, how their state is stored, and how they investigate failures — “celld is a love letter to their idea; a primitive this good deserves to run anywhere.”

This is only the acknowledgements for How Query Engines Work — Andy Grove thanks his family, "Mr. Powers" for "inspiring me to write this book in the first place," and the Apache Arrow and Apache DataFusion PMC members, committers, and contributors. It's a thin page with no table of contents or lessons: just a note that the book is "also available for purchase in ePub, MOBI, and PDF format" from Leanpub, plus a copyright line.

One of the most valuable things you could do for your software business is talk to your users — but Netlify's personalized onboarding email had a reply rate of just 1%, so they A/B tested cutting the text: down 75% to 37 words for a 4% reply rate, then down to 14 words for 8%. Compared to the original, the length was cut by 90% and reply rates increased by 700% — "the power of saying less." The advice: take your welcome email, cut what isn't necessary, take out another 50%, and run an A/B test.

“Small, sharp tools” — minimalist, composable programs that work in concert — is a principle Heroku folks borrowed from Unix and applied to modern web platforms, where it lines up with microservices. But Raymond’s *The Art of Unix Programming* warns of the “manularity trap”: tools that are too small force users to maintain shared context themselves, and “small, sharp tools in the Unix style have trouble sharing data” unless a framework makes communication easy. The author’s own lesson from re-integrating Heroku’s organizations service is that the Rule of Minimality means choosing the shared context first: “a tool can be too large *or* too small,” so build small only for more reason than size alone.

You've convinced the smartest investors, recruited a world-class team, and built the thing — then Roey stares back blankly: "you're, like, a gateway thing? We already have something for that." The most reliable fix is to "say something people want": accept that you probably don't know what they want, throw the traditional positioning playbooks in the trash, and talk to 30 of them about their aspirations, desired outcomes, and requirements instead of contrived categories like "AI Agent Composable Runtime Mesh Control Layer Firewall." Slack never featured the word "chat"; Slack, Wiz, Cloudflare, Fin, and Harvey win "by becoming known for *doing* something rather than for *being* something."

Kimaki is a "collaborative agent orchestrator" that turns Discord into the control surface for your coding agents: channels are projects, threads are sessions, and "you describe what you want, the agent does it, and the conversation lives in a thread you can return to." Setup is `npx -y kimaki@latest`, about a minute in Gateway mode using Kimaki's pre-built bot (self-hosted takes 5–10 minutes if you want full control over the bot identity), and it's "battle tested every day" by creator Tommy, who does all of his development through it. On billing it says you can "use your existing Claude Pro/Max and ChatGPT/Codex subscriptions instead of paying per token" — "Run `/login`, pick a provider, choose OAuth, and authenticate with your subscription."

Jan calls itself the "Open-Source ChatGPT Replacement" — "Your personal intelligence. Run any model, your way." It's "Free & Open source" with "7M+ downloads" and "Over 6 million downloads," and "is built in public" because "we believe AI should be open, and grow through the people who build and use it." v0.8.6 is now live on GitHub.

Lisse is "a small JavaScript library that draws squircle corners, the same continuous curve Figma and iOS use," with bindings for React, Vue, and Svelte plus a framework-agnostic core. Per-corner control, borders, and shadows are included.

The predictions land hard: "Code review will die," "the craft of writing code will disappear," and "tokens are the new computing paradigm." What survives is the craft of building software — knowing how to solve business problems with software, how other software did it and why and why not, when and how to ship it — while most bugs become "you asked for the wrong thing" bugs. Also declared dead: unit tests, the terminal, the PM/Design/Eng triad, and open source in its current form.

Manuel Muñoz Solera is "a designer from Villena, Alicante, based in beautiful California, building fun things at SpaceXAI," with photography as his longest-running hobby and guitar a close second. He's "having fun" with UnicodeKit ("Browsing characters like it's 1988"), Stray characters, Papercups ("My favorite compostable goods"), a Figma Orgchart ("I promise I'm fun at parties"), and GitHub Actions like the one that "does what it says on the tin."

The most common failure mode I've seen is the senior engineer death spiral: you try to cosplay being more senior, go quiet for two or three weeks, give the positive update at standup, then tell yourself you'll cram a month's work into a week and save it — and you start missing meals, losing sleep, and you burn out, get PIP'd, or quit. The fix is counterintuitive: drop a level and become the greatest teammate for a while, moving from an outcome-based mindset to a momentum-based one, because "big projects are not done with big efforts" — it's a marathon of slow, steady, incremental work. "Remember, you are in the reputation-building business, and software is actually downstream of that."

Being good at building and being good at shipping are two separate skills, and in the short term they're countervailing: "if you have a gift for building, you're likely to be *worse* at shipping." Gifted programmers freeze up because flaws in software bother them on an emotional level — they retreat to small domains where they can make code "correct" — while writers look at more than half their drafts and don't think they're very good. The only way around it is to "grit your teeth and ship it": you can't predict what people will find interesting, so you have to bias towards shipping and be momentum-based, not outcome-based.

, "Your team and agents, in the same room." hilos is a team chat where agents are members: ask for a change in a channel and "agents ship real PRs. Other agents review. People approve." hilos is free, and agents run on your machine, on your own account.

boat is "the cheapest, most powerful sandbox for agents, built for agent factories" by ASCII — a sandbox being "a persistent Linux (Ubuntu) virtual machine with SSH and SCP access, Docker support inside the VM, a dedicated IPv6 or IPv4 per machine, a 60fps virtual desktop, and fast disk-level forking from a snapshot." It's for AI agents, programmatic use, and humans — "Bring any agent: Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode" — with "Simple, honest pricing": a 7-day free trial (25 compute hours), then a $20/month minimum billed by the second, where $20 buys 2,000,000 VM-seconds across small (0.5x), default (1x), and large (2x) sizes. "No need to oversell boat. The product strives to speak for itself."

Equals is "a single source of truth for the entire team. Same question? Same answer." — a spreadsheet calculation layer on top of "all your GTM data synced and cleaned in a Snowflake instance we run for you," so you can "build dashboards and models" and answer questions about your business, with every figure traceable back to the source row. "Build once, iterate for years," then "wire your numbers into how your company operates" through scheduled Slack or email pushes, live charts in Notion, and calculated values pushed back into your CRM. Any agent connects over MCP to analyze the metrics your team trusts — not numbers it invented.

AI coding tools demand expertise to wield responsibly, yet they circumvent the friction — the failure, repetition, and getting "painfully stuck" — that actually builds that expertise, so the industry is sending mixed signals to novices who need expert-level taste to use tools that erode it. The fix isn't rejection but repurposing: "the most productive learning that can happen with an AI coding tool is when it isn't used to generate much of any code at all" — use them for interactive documentation, dynamic tutorial generation, and Socratic exercises, and keep the cognitive work on yourself. Because "LLMs are a static database of skills. They are interpolation engines... You cannot interpolate your way through a completely unique system failure."

Scritto is a JavaScript library that animates text in place: give an element a new value and "only the characters that changed move" — each one rolls from the old character to the new one while the rest hold their position. It works on numbers, words, and emoji, with bindings for React, Vue, Svelte, and Solid, "and a core that runs without a framework."

Highlighters is a small library that draws marker strokes over web text — “not a coloured box sitting behind the words, an actual stroke off a nib: ink that pools where a line starts and stops, streaks left behind as it dries, a little bleed past the last letter.” It never touches your text, so words stay selectable and searchable, marks hold their place through scrolling and resize, overlaps darken, and the library runs anywhere, with bindings for React, Vue and Svelte when you want them.

Cactus makes "Automation Foundation Models for Mobile, Wearables, AR glasses, Smart homes, Robotics, Automotive, Laptops, Game consoles, TVs, Microcontrollers" — "On-device intelligence on any hardware" in sub-30MB binaries, with 176k downloads/mo and 20k GitHub stars. Its latest releases include Needle 3, "a single 8–29 MB binary that beats models 10× its size on mobile tool calls," and Whistle, "a 16.9 MB open speech recognition model that supports seven languages and runs on CPU only," alongside sub-2-bit quantization, microprocessor-tier models that run "No GPU, no server, and no data leaving the device," and hybrid routing that sends low-confidence requests to the cloud. No pricing is shown on the page.

Modem "discovers and organizes your customer concerns" across support threads, sales calls, community posts, and social comments, then "groups what customers say into topics, then tracks the issues and pull requests working on each one." It's built for product, engineering, success, and sales teams, with a free tier of 2,500 events, Startup at $80/mo, Scale at $250/mo, and Enterprise custom — unlimited users on every plan and a 14-day free Scale trial.

Knap is a tool to "Turn data into Markdown": "Add variables inline with Markdown. Filters modify values and formatting." It runs conditionals, sorting, tables and YAML frontmatter — a cast list becomes a Markdown table, directors become wikilinks in properties — and you can "Generate Markdown from Knap templates" with the CLI (`npx knap render template.md --data data.json --output note.md`) or "Add Knap templating to your app using the API" (`npm install knap`). The page also points to Obsidian Web Clipper to "Save web pages to Markdown with customizable templates" and Obsidian Importer to "Convert data from many apps and file formats to portable Markdown files."

pgbot is “Postgres intelligence for AI agents & apps”: connect any PostgreSQL database and “Get answers, not dashboards” — what's healthy, what's broken, and what to fix first — with AI-powered explanations for health, query performance, tables, indexes, and changes.

It connects directly or runs an open-source agent next to private databases, and “pgbot mcp” speaks MCP on stdio so an AI agent can call pgbot as a read-only tool exposing deterministic tools like `inspect` and `unused_indexes`.

“pgbot never writes, so there's nothing an agent can break through it.”

Models.dev is an open-source database of AI models, with each row breaking out the Lab, Providers, Context, Output, whether it does Reasoning, Tool Call, Structured output and Temperature, its Weights (open, linked to Hugging Face, or Closed), Price, and release and updated dates. The table runs from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Mistral to DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax and Nvidia, and no rows match the current search.

Wellmade is "a home for well made creative work" — a feed of images from makers, which opens on a poster, "All In", "early identity concept", and "brand identity for pera". Visitors look: each thumbnail links straight out to the maker's post on the site.

A study of more than 64,000 people born in Britain between 1951 and 1956 found that less sugar exposure during the first 1,000 days — conception to a second birthday — meant a lower incidence of five cancers later in life: breast, prostate, liver, rectal and lung, with the effect strongest for liver cancer at around 69% lower and weakest for breast cancer at 36% lower. Those same people showed longer telomeres, equivalent to about 2.2 years of slower biological ageing, and lower levels of granzyme B. Most surprising is that "people who experienced sugar rationing early in life still consumed less sugar in adulthood, around age 50" — hinting at what the authors describe as two mechanisms, one biological and one behavioural, where a taste for less sweetness, formed early, seems to stick.

I rarely find good problems by blocking out time to "think strategically" — instead I act like a sponge, absorbing the problems people talk about in meetings, chat threads and 1:1s, and letting them sit in the back of my mind. Waiting can be a superpower: the same problem popping up independently in different teams is a higher priority, and several awkward requests may collapse into a single idea — though "a common shape is only a hypothesis and elegance is not evidence," so I pressure-test with prototypes, RFCs and conversations before building. The point is that finding problems worth solving isn't separate from the rest of the job; it comes from staying engaged with people's work long enough to see what no single request can show you.

AtAt is "your agent, in any app" — type @@ in any editable text field to ask your agent and put the answer right back where you type, with TabTab completing your next words across your Mac. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor and more, needs an Apple silicon Mac on macOS 15+, and starts with 7 days free, then $59 yearly or $169 lifetime with a 30-day refund promise. "Not another app to live in" — history stays on your Mac by default, with optional iCloud Sync that's off until you enable it.

Nautilus is a publication that covers science and its connections to culture, running pieces like "Can GLP-1s Slow Aging?" and "The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth." It publishes stories across categories including History, Biology, Arts, Math, and Communication, and offers a print edition, including "The Stupid Issue."

I am obsessed with smooth corners, so I built Lisse to draw the real Apple corner: a Bézier eased into an arc, not the superellipse that corner-shape ships. You hand it a radius and a smoothing value from zero to one per corner, and it reads the border and shadow you already wrote and redraws them as SVG that follows the curve around every edge, inner shadows included, instead of dropping them on the floor, with caching so five thousand identical corners cost about what fifty do. It is early, open source, MIT, there is a corne.rs site and a Chrome/Firefox extension, and I would like people to pull it apart and tell me where it breaks.

Building agents is still messy: we adopted the Vercel AI SDK for provider abstractions only and would not make that choice again, because the differences between models are significant enough that you need your own agent abstraction. Explicit cache management is now vastly preferred over platform-managed caching, reinforcement during the loop does more heavy lifting than expected, failures need strict isolation via subagents or context editing (which trashes caches), and a virtual file system is the building block that keeps tools from dead-ending. Output tooling is surprisingly tricky, model choice still depends on the task, and testing and evals remain the hardest problem — "we haven't found something that really makes us happy."

Artificial Analysis is "Independent analysis of AI" — compare models side-by-side on intelligence, pricing, speed, latency, benchmarks, and more so you can "understand the AI landscape to choose the best model and provider for your use case." It ranks and charts models through its own indices (Intelligence, Coding Agent, Cyber, Openness, Finance & Accounting), Image and Voice Arenas, cost-per-task and token pricing, output speed and latency, and provider endpoint comparisons on first-party APIs.

"Wondering turns anything you want to learn, from LLMs to quantum mechanics to product design, into a personalized course of three-minute lessons with visuals, podcasts, and interactive exercises." It's "a better habit than doomscrolling," gamified with daily streaks, friend streaks, XP for every lesson and streak freezes, and it works in five parts: bite-sized lessons, "watch, listen, or read," spaced repetition across everything you learn (scheduled with the FSRS algorithm), personalization to your goals and background, and an AI tutor to discuss anything. There's no FAQ or pricing here — just links out to public courses, a personalized AI course for your job, Canvas, a comparison page, and the iPhone download.

Delta is a multiplayer environment for coding with agents, where the unit of work is a thread: the conversation with an agent and the checkout of the repository it works in, kept together as one shareable artifact. Underneath it, DeltaDB is the version control layer that records work as a stream of fine-grained deltas, so a reference anchors to a change rather than a line number and survives as the code moves. Invite teammates into the same thread to review, comment, and work alongside the agent in real time.

Color encodes the kind of work, not the file, and when one color dominates that is usually the bottleneck: a mostly-yellow profile is CPU-bound on JavaScript. Line the network track up against the main thread, because if the thread is idle waiting on a bar you have a network problem and if it is solid with work while nothing downloads it is a CPU problem, and "self vs total is the distinction to internalize." Capture like your users first (CPU and network throttled, clean profile, cache off), then read in the order the guide works: Summary then Insights, Bottom-up sorted by self time, every red-cornered long task, a network cross-check, and finally verify the fix by checking the metric actually moved.

effect-mq packs "Schema-typed payloads, swappable storage, and at-least-once execution in one package" — jobs are schemas, handlers are Effects, workers are Layers, so "Interruption, retries, and timeouts run on the Effect runtime instead of bolted-on process machinery." Storage is a seam (Postgres through your drizzle schema, Redis through atomic Lua scripts, memory for tests), the producer/runner split means "Enqueueing never requires a Worker, and the type system enforces it," and it ships a run ledger, schedules with exactly-once ticks, dedup modes, cancellation, tracing and metrics. Install with `bun add effect-mq` or npm / pnpm / yarn.

Maggie Appleton is the author of these essays, from "A Treatise on AI Chatbots Undermining the Enlightenment" to "A Shelfish Starter Guide to Databases." Her work here includes "A Brief History & Ethos of the Digital Garden," "Tools for Thought as Cultural Practices, not Computational Objects," and "How to Draw Invisible Programming Concepts: Part I," a case study showing how she makes illustrations for abstract programming concepts. No socials or contact are shown on this page.

This one is thin: the page renders nothing but its title, **Learn Harness Engineering**, a logo, and a bare **Loading...** placeholder. There is no lesson, table of contents, FAQ, or price on the page to summarize — whatever it teaches isn't there yet.

Glaze lets you "Create any app in minutes by chatting with AI" — "Beautiful, powerful, and truly personal" desktop apps that are "Local-first" so they "run on your machine, no server or internet connection required." It's for anyone who can describe what they want, including teams building "Internal tools for your team, personal utilities, menu bar apps, workflow automations," and you can "Use a Claude subscription or Glaze credits to build." Available for macOS Tahoe and Apple Silicon, with "Windows and Linux will come down the road"; publishing to the public Glaze Store works on any plan, Team Stores are "free while Team Stores are in Beta," and "Pro adds unlisted publishing for 1:1 sharing."

The Pudding publishes visual data stories about "just about everything" — its own sticker reads "Visual Data Stories About Just About Everything" — numbered and dated like #225 Oct 2026 "life after death?", #224 Aug 2026 "mowing experiment", or #206 Jun 2025 "loneliness video", a six-minute video about the loneliness epidemic, in data. The stories run roughly monthly. You can "Get The Pudding in your inbox," and "Shop our swag."

This page is a directory of books — a cover image, a title, an author, and nothing else. It points to Guerra e Paz by Liev Tolstói, O Retrato de Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde, Autobiografia de um Iogue by Paramahansa Yogananda, Os Elementos by Euclides, Zero to One by Peter Thiel, Meditações by Marco Aurélio, Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari, and dozens more.

The most effective way to build software and get massive adoption is no longer high quality mainline apps but via building blocks that enable and encourage others to build quantity over quality. The factory of today is agentic, and AI is *really good* at gluing together high quality, well documented, and proven components — so the quality bar is lower, awareness is greater, the maintenance burden is lower, and R&D is outsourced. The mainline application becomes more stable and more purposeful in its feature set, while closed source commercial software appears to be at a massive disadvantage: the shift has already happened, we're living in it.

The LLM Inference Handbook calls itself "your technical glossary, guidebook, and reference - all in one," covering LLM inference from core concepts and performance metrics like Time to First Token and Tokens per Second to optimization techniques like continuous batching and prefix caching, GPU architecture, and deployment patterns like BYOC and on-prem. It is for engineers "deploying, scaling or operating LLMs in production," and it includes interactive calculators, simulators, and visual tools plus sections on Motivation, Who this is for, How to use this, Interactive tools, and Contributing.

Agents change the ROI on personalizing software on two fronts at once — it's much easier to get started and much easier to keep going, since a nightly cron job can fetch upstream changes and rebase your local ones — so software that can be personalized doesn't need a plugin system or a config file: "The source code is the extension system." For end-user products to make sense in a company today, they need to be personalizable, which means we need the source code. Where you hit a wall is Claude Code, because it's closed-source, so "If not, switch to an agent that lets you personalize it."

"Hey, I'm Alex. I'm super interested in software and design." He has been writing about software-related topics since 2019, with posts like "ASCII characters are not pixels: a deep dive into ASCII rendering," "A flowing WebGL gradient, deconstructed," "The web's clipboard, and how it stores data of different types," "Compressing Icelandic name declension patterns into a 3.27 kB trie," "Planes in 3D space," "Why doesn't TypeScript properly type Object.keys?" and "The Engineering behind Figma's Vector Networks." His writing is on /blog and you can learn about him on his /about page.

iris is "a camera for coding agents" — "One fast command or MCP tool call produces one trustworthy image," rendering with your real installed Chrome over the DevTools Protocol. It ships a CLI and a local stdio MCP server exposing one capture tool that returns pixels inline, and it's MIT-licensed, installed via a curl script or cargo install iris-screenshot, with an installed Chrome-family browser as its only runtime dependency.

Cold Takes publishes essays on AI timelines and alignment, the 'most important century,' utopia, and history, alongside 'Cold Links' roundups — each dated with a read time, from 'First Post' (3 min read) to 'Where's Today's Beethoven?' (25 min read). Recent items include a 'Cold Takes reader survey - let me know what you want more and less of!' and a 'Programming note'; the page itself lists no author, editor, or subscription details.

treg is “the tool catalog for your agent” — give this to your agent, and it gets a 3,900+ endpoint catalog with one unified key across 111 providers. No subscription, pay for results: price shown before the call, $1.00 free to start, bring your own key and those calls route through it unmetered. It’s 100% open source under AGPL, with credentials injected server-side, never on a machine.

Meet Okara, the AI CMO — "the only AI CMO you need for growth and marketing," with "10+ Marketing Agents Running 24/7" and "Used by 100,000+ users." It researches and prepares the strategy documents first (product-information, marketing-strategy, competitor-analysis, brand-voice, content-strategy), then its Influencer, Reddit, SEO, Writer, X, LinkedIn, GEO, Coding and UGC Videos agents execute channel by channel and publish straight into WordPress, Webflow, Framer, Wix, Sanity, GitHub, LinkedIn, X, WhatsApp, Telegram or Slack. "Free to start · No credit card required," and the paid tier is "From $129/mo" — the page calls it "The $14,000/mo job from $129/mo."

Articles is a running directory of bookmarks, each one a title and a line of description pointing outward — "The Bitterest Lesson," "Bored People Quit," "How to Earn a Billion Dollars." It wanders across code and design ("What if code wasn't the source?", "Designing with code," "Understanding Gradients") and scale ("118 million queries per second on Neki," "Making 768 servers look like 1").

Loop engineering is "replacing yourself as the person who prompts the agent" — you build a small system that finds the work, hands it out, checks it, and decides the next thing, and let that system poke the agents instead of you. A loop needs automations, worktrees, skills, plugins/connectors and sub-agents plus one place to remember stuff, and since Codex and Claude Code now ship all five, "you just design a loop that still works no matter which one you happen to be sitting in." The loop changes the work, it does not delete you from it: verification is still on you, comprehension debt grows faster, and "the comfortable posture is the dangerous one" — so build the loop, but build it like someone who intends to stay the engineer.

Wisereads is Readwise's "Weekly Wisereads" newsletter, archived here from "Wisereads Vol. 1 — A new newsletter by Readwise" up through Vol. 163. Each issue is listed by its contents, in the voice of headlines like "Wisereads Vol. 149 — The Plunge by Chris Ballard, Derek Thompson on the Enhanced Self, and more" or "Wisereads Vol. 139 — Laziness as a virtue, Anthropic's Mythos, and more." Nothing on the page names an editor or writer beyond the Readwise byline, and no subscription details are shown.

Pullfrog is a GitHub bot that runs AI agents on your repo — mention `@pullfrog` to review new PRs, auto-address new human reviews, triage/label issues, make plans, autofix CI, or autofix merge conflicts. It's open source with no per-seat pricing: "Personal accounts and public repositories stay free," with Organization at $30/month and custom Enterprise. Bring your own model — any LLM provider, or the Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT Codex, Grok, Kimi Code, or OpenCode Go plan you already pay for.

He asks his coding assistant to generate code in the chat and then manually makes every edit himself, keeping instructions in all his personal projects' agent files: "I want to understand every line of code that goes into this project. Never create, edit, move, rename, or delete project files unless I explicitly ask you to do so." Reviewing AI-generated PRs is "not fun" and personal projects "must be fun above all else," so he types every line to build a mental and spatial map of the codebase, catch hallucinations, and refactor to taste — "Instead of being 10x faster, I'm probably only 2x faster. But what I lose out on in terms of speed, I gain in terms of a deeper understanding of my code." It's the same learning process as the old advice to never copy and paste code, and while he fears the software industry is taking on "a large amount of cognitive debt that we'll have to pay back very soon," he can at least make sure he completely understands the software he puts out into the world.

"Training teaches a model what it knows. Inference is everything that happens afterward, every time somebody uses it, and it is where the bill actually lands." This is an interactive companion to *Inference Engineering* by Philip Kiely — "I rewrote the explanations and built simulators for the parts you grasp faster by turning a dial than by reading a paragraph" — and its structure is the book's: chapters plus a Glossary where "Every term, defined once." Beyond the intro, one sample simulator (Figure 1.4, time to first token versus tokens per second, with "Illustrative numbers") and an otherwise empty chapter list, the page is thin — no FAQ, no pricing, no word on what the chapters contain.

30,954 people mowed the same lawn and 'many came close to the optimal path' — 16% did it perfectly, and the median person hit 91% efficiency. Unlike the Traveling Salesman research, optimality held around 90% whether the lawn took 26 moves or 177, because a lawn has structure that lets people decompose it into sections and compress what they learn. And it's not about thinking more or faster, but when thinking happens: the best mowers spent their pauses at the forks and dead ends, then cruised through the rest.

The mind that builds software is far smaller than the software it builds — four slots, a narrow beam, and a leak — and "almost everything good in engineering is a way of living with that gap." Read that way, "human error" gets harsher light: a warning half of attentive people look straight at and never see "isn't really a warning. It's a decoration," and every system built for an operator who never gets tired "is already broken. It just hasn't had its bad day yet." The machines repeat the pattern — a context window that goes "lost in the middle," more retrieved documents pulling accuracy down — so the question isn't how to find a mind big enough, it's "how do we shape the thing so that a small mind can work on it without bringing it all down."

Learn to Cloud is a free, open-source, self-paced program — "We provide the path, practice, and feedback; you bring the agency and discipline to build a lasting career." Its structure is three promises: learn with direction (structured curriculum, resources, practical challenges, clear goals, community), improve with feedback (automated checks and AI-assisted reviews), and learn what's current (updated by people working in the field). You start with Linux and networking, build an AI-powered API, then deploy, automate, and secure that same application on your chosen cloud.

In my day to day as a software developer I often switch between different code repositories, and I don't want to remember whether it was `./gradlew build` or `mvn`, `yarn` or `npm` — "I want to be able to say *'build the code'*, *'lint it'*, *'format it'*, *'run migrations'*, *'install dependencies'*." So I look at a few ways to pull this off, from good old bash scripts and `make` (mind the tabs, declare your `.PHONY` targets) to more modern task runners like `just` and `mise`, all so you can apply muscle memory to the things you do a dozen times each day. It's not exactly rocket science — a small quality of life improvement for you and your team that's super simple to set up and yet something I rarely see in the wild.

A numbered love letter to the personal website — 95 reasons, from "to write for oneself" and "to have a home on the open web" to "to keep the like counter at 0," "because vibe coding only gets you so far," "to bring web rings back," and "to remember that a website is just files & folders." It runs the whole range: "as a form of prayer," "as a form of protest," "to make a soup," "to document a ufo sighting." And then, at the end, the question: "do we need a reason to website?"

This is "not preaching absolute truth but merely some personal preferences and understandings of what makes a good React component": name props without duplicating context (`isOpen`, not `isDialogOpen`), derive booleans from existing props instead of bolting on an `isClosable`, and reach for enum props so that impossible states are impossible. Composability wins over a giant `data` prop — low-level compound components like Radix's give you control over every element rendered, and "Yikes" to the alternative that loses JSX. For high-frequency interactions, if other parts of your interface don't rely on the state, update the element directly from the callback rather than triggering a re-render.

Two recent Silicon Valley stories are hard to read without wondering if everyone involved has lost their mind — a couple earning $550,000 that still feels behind, and a founder who has Claude review her first dates to judge whether she was engaging enough. "People fear being replaced by machines and respond by giving those machines more of their judgment, attention and time," every saved hour returned to "a race with no finish line." If the valley shows us what it means to live in the future, perhaps falling behind is not the worst thing that could happen — maybe we need the misfits who know when to stop.

Artificial intelligence can do more every day, but deciding what it should do is up to us: "the future worth building is human — shaped by human knowledge, guided by human will, and decided by human judgment." Because productive knowledge is tacit, local, and held by the people who acquire it through their work — intelligence alone only suffices in domains with static goals and no hidden knowledge, like chess and math — AI must be as diverse and distributed as the people it serves, trained on their unique knowledge and aligned in its weights rather than frozen in a handful of places. Human participation and capability, ownership and safe alignment, are framed as technical challenges to solve: interaction models that carry live multimodal feedback, tools for fine-tuning and customization, and an ecosystem of AIs "raised in different places, disagreeing, competing, and learning from each other."

Spotted in Prod is "The very best of iOS" — a collection of community clips of app interfaces, tagged by design language (System, Minimal, Skeuomorphism, Colorful, Loud, Retro, Liquid Glass, Brutalist, Pixel Art and more) and by visual, gesture, flow, pattern, category and team type. A visitor browses clips like "Museum" by reactiive to watch taps, scrolls, swipes, morphs, onboarding, paywalls and app icons up close on the screen.

Invisible Details is "the resource I was looking for years ago and couldn't find": two chapters, Notes then Practice — first the theory (states, feedback, inputs, speed), then "watching it getting applied" to a single component, examining "every single decision, the trade-offs behind it and alternatives of doing it in other places." You've felt all of this already, you just haven't been shown it — read a few chapters for free, then it's a one-time purchase, forever yours, with a 40% off regional price for India.

“Hi, I’m Justin. These are my articles.” The page is a long-running index of his writing — year-in-review posts, essays like “Do the hardest thing” and “Avoid fame,” and pieces on SaaS, marketing, podcasting, bootstrapping, AI, coding, and being a founder — with no bio, socials, or contact shown beyond the article links and a Statamic credit.

Its cards run from "AI & Design: A shift in how we design" and "Designing Articless: A thought process on articless" to "Design Thinking: Design better interfaces," "The Basics: Improving quality & taste," "Typography: The beauty of design" and "Simple Interfaces: Hide complex thinking." No socials or contact are shown.

There's no secret silver bullet: Linear is fast because it's built from the ground up on the right foundation, then improved by countless decisions — the database lives in the browser, mutations apply locally first and reconcile in the background, and the server is a sync target rather than a source of truth for the UI. The first load ships less code in more pieces with a service worker precaching the rest while you sit on the login page, auth is assumed and verified later, and per-property MobX observables mean a 50-issue update is 50 cell re-renders rather than a list re-render. Add keyboard-first design and animations that stay on the GPU with durations below the 100ms cause-and-effect threshold, because as the piece keeps saying, "the secret to building incredible web apps is by hiding all the network requests from the user."

Feather is an inbox that "Removes what's done, keep what matters, and nudges what needs you" — sorting, merging, and surfacing insights "on its own." No pricing, free tier, or open-source status is shown on the page.

Hatchet is "the orchestration engine for teams who ship" — write tasks and workflows as code in TypeScript, Python, or Go, then run workers on your own infrastructure while the engine runs as a managed service or self-hosted. It's "fully MIT-licensed" (running it locally is "a single CLI command away") and it "replaces your home-grown cron systems, legacy data pipelines, and overly complex orchestration providers with a single, easy-to-use platform."

Great interfaces rarely come from a single thing. They're usually a collection of small things that compound into a great experience. — so here are the details Jakub uses: `text-wrap: balance` on titles and `text-wrap: pretty` on descriptions, concentric border radii where "the outer radius equals the inner radius plus the padding," contextually animated icons, `antialiased` for crispy macOS text, `tabular-nums` for numbers that don't shift, interruptible animations ("CSS transitions are great for interactions, while keyframe animations are better for staged sequences that run once"), split and staggered enter animations, subtler exits, optical rather than geometric alignment, and shadows or a 10% outline instead of borders.

Library is "the infrastructure your design system runs on" — components, tokens, and patterns read at the source from Figma and code, kept live at a URL your team can browse and ask questions of in plain language, "for your team today, for your agents tomorrow." Try it free for 30 days, then $15 per editor / month with unlimited viewers — AI answers are billed separately, priced per token.

It's aimed at designers and content creators, with "Whirrrrls" chanting between testimonials from basit.designs, supercharge.design, and ux.alok. The only call to action is a "Get Now" button; no price, free tier, or open-source status appears on the page.
Break down CSS backgrounds, layer by layer — paste any background CSS and see what each layer contributes, separately. In the playground you can drag to reorder layers and try an example.

Built by founder Jim Raptis for Twitter branding and landing-page visuals, it promises "a streamlined editing process" that "doesn't force you to mess around with frames, layers, artboards, and other complex elements."

Everyone can ship things today, but most of what gets shipped cannot survive — survival is the real test, and it isn't about profitability, PMF, or DAU. Simplicity is the survival strategy: "Simplicity does not mean faster progress. It means less surface area for decay." So make better things, not more things, and ship slowly — patient iterative improvement compounds, and "less hustle means less hype and more craft."

A border-radius is just a number, and roundness is relative — the same 12px reads soft on a small button and nearly disappears on a wide card, and nested corners still won't line up. The rule for nesting is that "the inner radius is the outer radius minus the gap," with the border counted as part of the gap, so you "write the relationship, not the result." But that subtraction only works because the default corner is a quarter circle — with `corner-shape` squircles, "the formula was always a floor, not a finish," so judge the result and ship the least-wrong one.

Quality is “the absence of problems”, best measured by having many experts take a look — a spectrum up to a perfection that's impossible, where “the closer you try to get to perfection, the harder it is.” It comes down to organisational ability and appetite (“~100% of the time I've seen an organisation make high quality software, it is because the leaders wanted it”), which is why quality gets harder with scale and is impossible past a certain point — a trade-off, not a problem to be solved. In software the signals are reliability, speed, clarity, efficacy, efficiency, and beauty; quality isn't necessary, but “everyone wants to live in a higher-quality world.”

Watchmaking is jargon-heavy, but "you shouldn't feel pressured to remember" the names — every part is color-coded.

Master process."

The crux: 'if you're working hard as a generalist on a project you care a lot about, then by rigorously applying the lessons from these documents you will improve more quickly than you otherwise would.' If you read only one item, make it Anna Salamon's 'Humans are not automatically strategic', because 'it's good to understand the ways in which otherwise-intelligent people are unstrategic' and the ways in which you are not automatically strategic.

Slop creep is "the slow, invisible enshittification of a codebase through an accumulation of individually reasonable but collectively destructive decisions," and coding agents removed the old circuit breaker: an agent "can keep piling crap on top of more crap, indefinitely, and stay productive the entire time," so the reckoning is deferred, compounded and worse. The problem is that agents "see the prompt" and not the system, so they are "confidently, competently wrong" — correct in isolation, wrong for the system — and the response is not to stop using them but to put ten times more attention into the plan, with actual code snippets for data models and key interfaces, because "the agent should never be the one walking through a one-way door alone."

Every item currently listed is a placeholder — "An Example Post Title" with lorem ipsum body text, dated "January 1, 0000" and credited to "Example Author" — and the page shows no cadence or subscription details.

Apple's Liquid Glass at WWDC inspired Aave to bring the same effect to its mobile apps, and this is the story of bringing it to the web: "Our technique runs in every modern browser, on desktop and on mobile, with no flags to turn on and no fallbacks to maintain. It just works." The glass bends the real rendered content rather than a copy of it — a single SVG filter primitive, `feDisplacementMap`, driven by a map generated from the glass's shape — which is "why text under the lens stays selectable and links stay clickable," and when there's no live DOM to bend, like a canvas-drawn QR code or a video Safari refuses to filter, "the same map feeds a WebGL shader instead. The renderer changes with the medium, the refraction stays the same." Most of the work went into Safari: giving the filter a fresh ID on every update so it doesn't "freeze mid-motion," computing only a quarter of the map via four-fold symmetry, staying conservative with the DOM footprint, and reading a small lens-sized region for the specular highlight.

Design keeps being misunderstood as the act of producing — but "the hard part of design is rarely generating the form. It is understanding the problem well enough to know what and how something should exist at all." Christopher Alexander's good fit between form and context is the real work, and AI's fast, plausible outputs don't help you get there: "The form is there. The fit is not." That's why the author still prefers designing visually over prompting — the value is "not only in the output," but the gradual understanding that comes through doing the work.

Coding agents are sirens, luring you in with breakneck code generation, and after 12 months everything is broken: booboos compound with no human bottleneck, agents are "merchants of complexity" who never learn, and agentic search has low recall, so you end up with an unrecoverable mess of complexity in weeks instead of years. The fix is to slow the fuck down — let the clanker do the boring, scoped, evaluable stuff while you stay the final quality gate, hand-write anything that defines the gestalt of your system, and "set yourself limits on how much code you let the clanker generate per day, in line with your ability to actually review the code." "Learning to say no is a feature in itself."

Browser agents turn prompt injection from saying something wrong into doing something wrong, and "every webpage an agent visits is a potential vector for attack." You can't patch the web, so Browserbase's mitigation is containment — each session runs in a dedicated VM with hardware virtualization isolation, isolated subnets and strict firewalls, killed and recreated after every session — plus Stagehand's "safe, deterministic automation" as a guardrail, with the LLM used only as a fallback for edge cases. The bet: keeping the scope of potential damage small "when (not if) the web tries to talk your agent into going rogue."

A categorized index of software engineering laws, each stated in one line — from Conway's Law ("Organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structure") to Sturgeon's Law ("90% of everything is crap") — grouped under Planning, Architecture, Quality, Design, Teams, Scale, and Decisions. Movement tells a story: well-designed motion makes a UI both more engaging and more intuitive, while bad transitions and animations can make the same UI feel mediocre, cheap, confusing, or even broken — possibly "worse than no movement at all." At the center of any movement on the web is the easing curve, the "rhythm" of the movement, which is a cubic bézier curve — "a line, usually curved, defined by four numeric values" — where the horizontal x axis is the duration of the transition and the vertical y axis is the speed of the change. "The transition itself is the verb; the easing curve is the adverb."

There's career advice that sounds obvious but is chronically underrated: the product you work on matters more than the title on your badge — a frontend engineer should work where the frontend *is* the product, and a backend engineer the reverse. The test is where the complexity lives: thin client/thin server products "don't stretch anyone" (and "AI is able to generate these easily these days"), while thick client/thick server products like Figma, Google Docs and Spotify are where "everyone here is solving hard problems" — "You want to be here." Get it wrong and you're wiring API responses to form fields or maintaining "a glorified database proxy," a gap that compounds over years and often arrives as a "bait and switch" where the X you were hired for never materializes.

His career also runs through Summation, Fused, Profound, and National Defence, where he was a DevSecOps Lead Architect, Software Developer, and Software Developer Intern, and he's reachable by mail, GitHub, LinkedIn, or a booked call.

No editor, writer, cadence, or subscription details are shown on the page.

Every interface that's ever felt right had something in common: it respects how I actually think, not how a spec says I should. So I walk through the laws I keep coming back to — Fitts's (make the things people need to click easy to click), Hick's (progressive disclosure, show what matters now), Miller's (chunking isn't a nice-to-have, it's a cognitive necessity), the Doherty Threshold (if you can't make something fast, make it feel fast), and Postel's (validate generously, format strictly). They're not really about interfaces, they're about how people work — and "the hardest thing to do is make something feel easy."

Slim gives your localhost a local or public URL: turn `localhost:3000` into `https://app.test` with path routing, HTTPS, HMR support, or get a public URL without deployment. “Free Forever · Built with Go.” It’s a single Go binary for local domains, internet sharing, commands like `slim start`, `slim list`, and `slim doctor`, with CA, per-domain certs, `/etc/hosts`, port forwarding, and reverse proxying handled under the hood; install with `curl -sL https://slim.sh/install.sh | sh` or build from source on GitHub.

Because LLMs are "stateless functions" and CLAUDE.md "is the only file that by default goes into every single conversation you have with the agent," it should onboard Claude to your codebase with the project's WHY, WHAT and HOW — using as few instructions as possible, since "as instruction count increases, instruction-following quality decreases uniformly" and Claude Code's own system prompt already eats ~50 of the ~150-200 instructions a frontier model can reliably follow. Keep it "concise and universally applicable" (HumanLayer's root file is "less than sixty lines"), practice progressive disclosure by pointing to separate docs with file:line references rather than stuffing in code snippets, and don't send Claude to do a linter's job: "Never send an LLM to do a linter's job." Avoid /init and auto-generation, because "`CLAUDE.md` is the highest leverage point of the harness."

Writing code used to be the slow half of the work, and now that AI makes creation cheap, the queue is the problem: OpenClaw has north of 2,500 open PRs, and "if input grows faster than throughput, you have an accumulating failure." You can throttle the inflow like Pi, which auto-closes PRs unless people are trusted, or give in and let machines review machines — but "non-sentient machines will never be able to carry responsibility," so the bottleneck is still a person. "I too am the bottleneck now. But you know what? Two years ago, I too was the bottleneck. I was the bottleneck all along."

Before and after is a skill that will "Put visual proof in every pull request" by teaching coding agents to "show their work with before and after screenshots and video." It navigates browser flows, handles authentication, captures media, and "format[s] every capture for GitHub," with navigation, authentication and capture left to the version-matched skills bundled in `agent-browser` while it formats the media and publishes it through `gh --attach`. Install it with `npx skills add vercel-labs/before-and-after#main`.

Typex zeigt eine Tastatur mit „Linker Mittelfinger“ und Buchstabenfolgen wie „dalk·salsa·das·flak“; die Aufforderung lautet: „Tippe die Buchstaben ab“. Zu Zielgruppe, Preis, Free Tier oder Open Source steht auf der Seite nichts.

DesEngs is a directory of Resources for Design Engineers, linking out to articles, libraries, components, jobs and community pages — from "A tool to calculate perfect nested border radii" to "Design Engineering Community." The through-line is the design-engineering seam the page states plainly: "Design and code work hand-in-hand to produce memorable digital products."

Three algorithms answer the questions that make rate limiting tricky: fixed windows are "simple to implement and understand" but "allow bursts up to 2x the `limit`," sliding windows smooth traffic but get resource-intensive, so real-world limiters like Cloudflare and Upstash use a floating-window approximation — `(prevWindowCount * prevWindowWeight) + currentWindowCount`. Token buckets separate burst capacity from the refill interval, which "represents the long-term average allowed request interval" (Stripe, OpenAI, and the post's Twitch chat demo all use them). Wherever you land: persist the store outside memory, fail open, key on user ID or API key, and return 429 with `x-ratelimit-*` headers.

Jakub Krehel is a founding design engineer at Interfere, "where we're building the self-healing layer of the internet," and previously worked at OpenSea and a few other companies. He cares deeply about craft and quality and likes to make people feel something through his work, writing notes, thoughts and pieces on UI, animations and colors. You can reach him at @jakubkrehel, via email, or see his code on GitHub.

Saying taste is subjective is a good way to prevent disputes, but it's not true — if there's no such thing as beauty, designing things is a job you can never get better at, and yet you do. So Graham treats beauty as a practical question, *how do you make good stuff?*, and finds the same principles of good design cropping up in math, painting, software, and writing: it's simple, timeless, suggestive, hard, looks easy, uses symmetry, resembles nature, is redesign, can copy, is often strange, happens in chunks, and is often daring. "The recipe for great work is: very exacting taste, plus the ability to gratify it."

AI can write animation code, but what it can't do is know what feels *right* — "It produces motion that works, but feels mediocre, and if you can’t tell the difference, you’ll ship it." The fix is training your eye: each exercise shows two animations side by side, you pick the better one and write down why, then see the breakdown — and "putting into words why something feels right trains your ability to articulate your judgment, a skill that will be incredibly valuable in the AI era."

A behind-the-scenes walkthrough of crafting interface sounds for three interactions — a library card pull-down, a scratch-to-reveal, and a last-minute Claude gift animation — built from real recorded source material like a date stamp, gift cards scratched with a quarter, and resampled drum loops. Each moment gets layered beats: a quick snap if the pull doesn't pass threshold, a bright chime and tactile click once the card slots in, and "a warm full chord that sustains into the next step." The closing note: "Sound is easy to overlook, especially in digital products, but I hope moments like these show how much it can add."

I can't overstate how much I hate GitHub Actions — with a capitalized Passion that's "one degree above regular passion" — mostly because one system in a four-target matrix failing meant a 2–3 minute loop of search, push, open the Actions tab, and hate life, "FOR. A. SINGLE. CHANGE." The takeaway is the internet's wise saying: "**For the love of all that is holy, don't let GitHub Actions manage your logic. Keep your scripts under your own damn control and just make the Actions call them!**" So I deleted `build.rs`, moved all the generation into a GNU Makefile, and called it a day — "…but at least I dodged the bullet early."

Entire is a Git hosting platform — "The fastest Git network on Earth" — where agents clone and push to your repositories up to 89 times faster than the competition, built on the first principle that "all features are available through the CLI." Every commit an agent makes becomes a checkpoint paired with the conversation behind it, sessions sync with your Git history, secrets are detected and redacted before anything is stored, and the semantic graph is "100% local and open source." The CLI works with any agent and is open source under the MIT license.

Forma is "a native MacOS app with a focus on design, built by a product designer" that puts notes and tasks on a spatial canvas — "project boards, freeform notes, or your own system, right on your Mac." It is "not free — it is a one-time purchase of $9.99 with no subscription," there's no free trial, it's sold through the Mac App Store (refunds via Apple's standard process), and everything is stored locally with iCloud sync on by default.

I'm a Brand Designer at Vercel, working across brand, web, and code in the devtools space, and before that I was at LiveKit and Supabase, "where I helped shape their brand and websites as they grew." Based in Croatia, I co-run Buka Studio with my partner (and a cat who rarely skips meetings), and I'm still brewing cfntd.site, a small coffee archive for specialty coffee enthusiasts, plus a Digital Stamp Collection "paying homage to my grandpa's lifelong passion for philately." For anything else, Let's talk.

There are two kinds of AI users now — power users all in on Claude Code, MCPs, skills, "often *not very technical*" — and everyone else who is still just chatting to ChatGPT. Enterprise IT is the disaster zone: locked-down environments, no internal APIs, siloed engineering, and Copilot as often the only allowed tool, which is "slow" and whose agent feature is "absolutely laughable" compared to a CLI coding agent — while Microsoft itself rolls out Claude Code internally. Meanwhile small companies are "*absolutely flying*," and "I don't think there's ever been a time in history where a tiny team can outcompete a company one thousand times its size so easily."

The essay takes playful questions like "was Darwin a writer?" seriously to examine what Brand, Darwin, and Einstein are really doing, and concludes that new creative identities emerge "often from the work of near-amateurs" — people who begin with a fundamental question no existing field takes seriously, then deploy every tool they can find to answer it. Identity *matters*, and forging a replacement for a lost one "often requires leaving existing communities, and becoming illegible even to oneself for a time"; writing is a mutable, extensible tool that evolves in concert with new ways of understanding, not a fixed genre. The point is to hold the tension rather than resolve it, and to keep exploring the practices of different creative people.

Echo is "the fast & modern SSH + Mosh client for iOS & iPadOS that makes the mobile terminal a pleasure" — connect, execute, and automate from your pocket, with native Keychain, Face ID, Metal-accelerated rendering, Mosh support that keeps sessions alive on patchy signal, and 400 themes. Built for iPhone & iPad (iOS 26+), it costs $2.99 on the App Store, and its "minimal, distraction-free UI is the perfect environment to interact with coding agents on the go."

Halftone started as a printing workaround for limited ink colors but now it's "a versatile artistic tool used across media and the web to give some kind of texture or grain to digital outputs" — and I've spent the past few months trying the different flavors it can take, breaking each one down in GLSL so that building and designing with halftone is more approachable. I walk through rendering a grid of dots with `fract` and distance fields, applying it as a filter with luma-based radii and offsets, then the multichannel stuff — Moiré patterns, subtractive vs additive blending, and a CMYK halftone where each layer gets its own rotation to keep the artifacts down. Then I break the grid entirely: cell-wall sampling across a 3x3 kernel, gooey ink-like dots that merge with `smoothmin`, and displaced dots driven by a mouse trail, because "from a very simple shape like a circle, we can quickly branch off to a diverse set of effects, each more interesting and pleasing than the other."

Pool "knows what actually matters" — it "magically links and categorises your content… that you can organize in pools and share with friends." It's an iOS app you download on the App Store as "Pool: Capture Anything," alongside Research and Careers pages; the page shows no pricing, free tier, or open-source status.

Suspense can pause a component's DOM updates, ensuring smoother exit animations — the problem being that updates triggering exit animations often affect the exiting component's contents too, and React batches them with the update that closes the popover. Digging around, he found React continues to render suspended subtrees but doesn't commit their changes to the DOM, so he built a small `Freeze` wrapper around Suspense that un-applies its `display: none !important` style via a Fragment ref and an insertion effect, which he's used in a few projects. It's "obviously a bit of a trick" that could break in a future version of React, though it worked in React 18 & 19.2.

The Option Method, created by Bruce Di Marsico in the 1970s, holds that unhappiness is never necessary — it is always optional: "you are unhappy because you think you should be." Change the beliefs that create it and "the unhappiness evaporates," because happiness is your natural state, "always accessible to you if you can just drop the belief that something else needs to happen first" — no circumstance has to change first. The essay walks through the Socratic questioning steps, reads unhappiness as a distorted signal of what you deeply value, and answers the objections: it's a terrible motivator, it isn't spiritual bypass, and it doesn't mean your depression is your fault.

Erik Johannes Husom accepts Andy Masley's point that we won't drain a finite pool of thinking, but argues the "lump of cognition" framing misses what actually matters: the categories where outsourcing thinking is harmful — personal communication, valuable experiences, tacit knowledge — are far larger than Masley's list suggests, because "the words *are* the meaning." He also rejects the extended mind outright ("simply absurd"), insisting that memorizing knowledge is a huge part of learning to use it, and closes on values: "there are good reasons for protecting certain human activities against the automation of machines," since how we use chatbots "is not only about efficiency and cognitive consequences; it's about how we want our lives and society to be."

Most components are built for the happy path: they work until they don't, and the real world is hostile, with server rendering, hydration, multiple instances, concurrent rendering, async children, and portals all waiting to break them. Walking through a single theme provider, Shu Ding makes it server-proof, hydration-proof, instance-proof, concurrent-proof, composition-proof, portal-proof, transition-proof, activity-proof, leak-proof, and future-proof, moving browser APIs into useEffect, injecting a synchronous script before paint, swapping cloneElement for context, reaching for ownerDocument.defaultView, and tainting server-only values. "These aren't edge cases. They're the new normal."

A digital playbook of 175+ tactic cards sorted into 12 stacks, where each card is "an emotional building block, designed to make your feature land and your app stick" — delivered as a huge Figma swipe file with 99+ real app screens. It's for "anyone building experiences in the consumer app space": founders, designers, developers, product managers, growth marketers. "Pay once, $97, download it straight away. No subscription. Updates are free forever."

*The Crux* is a "fantastic follow on" to *Good Strategy, Bad Strategy* — same core ideas in a more readable format, with "a clearer target to take down: the incoherent outputs of process and goal-driven strategy." Its recurring themes: "Don't start with goals–start by understanding the challenge and finding its crux," and "Don't Confuse Current Financial Results with Strategy," since the financial lens is reassuring because "the numbers always add up" but "provides guardrails but it doesn't actually tell us what to do." Rumelt treats strategy as design and creation rather than deduction — "a design rather than a choice... a creation embodying purpose" — and I'd still recommend *Good Strategy, Bad Strategy* first if you only read one.

Agentation is a toolbar you activate with the icon in the bottom-right corner — hover over elements to see their names highlighted, click any element to add an annotation, then "click to copy formatted markdown" and paste it into Claude, Codex, Gemini, Grok, or any coding agent with access to your codebase. Where you'd otherwise "describe the element ('the blue button in the sidebar') and hope the agent guesses right," it hands over CSS selectors, source file paths, the React component tree, computed styles, and your feedback with intent and priority. "Agentation is free for individuals and companies for internal use," with a commercial license by contact if you're redistributing it as part of a product you sell.

Make It Animated is a collection of React Native animations and components pulled from real-world mobile apps — "Battle-tested patterns optimized for 60fps performance using Reanimated, Gesture Handler, Animated API & Skia" — with detailed comments so you can "copy the code, understand the patterns, and ship better user experiences faster." It offers 70+ animations plus production-ready components like Loader, Shimmer, and TextStrikethrough, with a simple deal: "US$59 one time payment plus local taxes" for lifetime access, next price US$69. Subjects: react, animation, components, mobile, motion.

We asked how Letta would do on LoCoMo by simply placing the conversational history into a file and giving the agent filesystem tools — grep, search_files, open, close — and "this simple agent achieves 74.0% on LoCoMo with GPT-4o mini and minimal prompt tuning, significantly above Mem0's reported 68.5% score for their top-performing graph variant." (Mem0's earlier numbers claiming MemGPT on LoCoMo were puzzling to the team behind MemGPT, and Mem0 "did not respond to requests for clarification.") The argument is that whether an agent "remembers" something depends on whether it can use a retrieval tool effectively, so "simpler tools are more likely to be in the training data of an agent and therefore more likely to be used effectively" — agent capabilities matter more than the tools, and comparing frameworks to memory tools is apples to oranges.

After a lucky duck took the last Lyft bike — again — I spent the next month reverse engineering Lyft's private API, bypassing SSL encryption with Charles Proxy, replaying the geofenced `rent` endpoint with spoofed coordinates, and brute-forcing five-digit bike IDs with asyncio at ~650 RPS ("I promise it's not a Denial of Service Attack"), which unlocked one bike, sometimes two. Then came the sev email, the HackerOne report ("Proof of Concept: Trivial"), and a $500 bounty — so I'm writing it up in case you might learn too. "Curiosity and determination are unreasonably effective... Go reverse engineer something. Just, be nice about it."

Knowing nothing about audio engineering, he funneled the dense Web Audio API docs into Cursor and talked his way to a sound library: filter noise with a bandpass and it becomes a click, shape it with envelopes because real sounds decay exponentially, not linearly — describe what's wrong, listen, repeat. "I provided taste and AI provided implementation. Neither of us could have done it alone." Turns out "sometimes not knowing the technicalities is actually a good thing."

A Zajno motion-design lesson arguing that UI/UX animation "emphasizes the details to which users should pay attention" and "captures the mood of a brand or product," structured as an intro on interaction (interactive vs. not real-time), a techniques section, then Lesson 1, "THE BASICS OF EASING" — linear, ease, ease-in, ease-out, cubic — with Dribbble implementation examples (Fly Dashboard, Keep Website, PalmPalm) and the classic slow-in-slow-out car demo: "Applying this principle gives your objects more life." Most agent files fail because they're too vague — "'You are a helpful coding assistant' doesn't work. 'You are a test engineer who writes tests for React components, follows these examples, and never modifies source code' does." Across 2,500+ `agents.md` files, the ones that work give the agent a specific persona, put executable commands early, show real code snippets over explanations, name the stack with versions, and set three-tier boundaries — hitting six core areas: commands, testing, project structure, code style, git workflow, and boundaries. Start with one specific task, test it, and add detail when your agent makes mistakes, because "the best agent files grow through iteration, not upfront planning."

Paper is a browser-based design tool focused on the early, exploratory phase of design, giving designers "a fast, expressive canvas to think visually, experiment freely, and play with things like shaders, gradients, and motion without worrying about handoff or engineering constraints." Founder Stephen Haney argues that design and engineering are different jobs, and that tools which "introduce coding or responsive constraints too early can actually be harmful in that early part of the process." Under the hood it's built hard for speed — an 8 millisecond frame budget (around 120fps), MobX, Bun, Hono, MongoDB, hand-written shaders, and a homegrown WebSocket multiplayer system — so you can copy the exact code that's running straight onto the canvas output.

It sells an All Access Pass at $269 USD/year (team pricing $1,199 USD/year) with a 30-day money-back guarantee, no free trial but several free videos, and self-contained videos averaging 7–10 minutes that you can take "with a full-time job." Coding agents are only as good as their feedback loop, so give your agent a laboratory, not a task — the ability to view and verify its own work. If the agent ever asks you to do something manually, "you should 1) stop 2) think really *really* hard about how to give the agent the tools it needs so it can do the thing by itself." The prompt examples reorient the mental model: build a benchmark harness before touching code, then loop — screenshot, compare, "fix them one by one, verifying each fix in the browser" — until you can't find any differences.

"Novelty is the equivalent of an exclamation mark. Akin to seasoning, you don't want too much of it" — the more commonly an action is performed, the less rewarding any extravagant animation or visual flourish on it becomes, semantic satiation applied to interfaces. Borrowing the three color rule from cinematography, the proposal is to make 90% of the experience familiar and 10% novel, treating novelty as the accent color: dialed up for onboarding, a staggered first load, or a microsite like Stripe Press, and absent on the return trip, because "novelty works best as a contrast. It becomes overwhelming otherwise." What you can get away with depends on *intent* and the "novelty tax" — Arc "built Arc into a saxophone, but found it challenging to transform into a piano" — so the takeaway is simply: "Make most things familiar, do something unexpected."

I write to organize my own mind, and I've been losing sleep over LLMs, so here's the one thread I pulled out: value comes in two kinds. Utility is what a thing actually does, but meaning comes from spending an irreplaceable fraction of your life in service of another — "the more we automate the process of making a thing, the less of ourselves we put into it." Generative AI "can transmute that former kind of value into the latter," draining meaning while letting you make more useful things for the same effort, but "it can't generate meaning," so I aim to use it for utilitarian goods and put as much of myself and as little of the machine as I can into the things where human connection matters.

Effect is "TypeScript's missing standard library" — errors are *values* the compiler tells you about, so try-catch pyramids and `Promise.all` death traps get replaced by built-in retries, timeouts, interruption, and resource cleanup. It's "functional programming without the gatekeeping" ("No monad lectures. No category theory homework."), production-ready and API stable at v3.0, and via `@effect/ai` it's "literally built for" LLM agents — provider-agnostic across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Bedrock, with structured concurrency and real tests instead of "I hope this works in prod" prayers. Commands are dead, absorbed into skills and subagents, and "both skills and MCP - when used incorrectly - will cause context pollution in your harness." The ask is simple: stop with "X is all you need," go try skills and some *good* MCP servers, because the real skill is managing your context window.

You can pursue genuine intellectual curiosity with a full-time job and scattered hours, and the constraint isn't credentials or time — it's knowing how to scope questions, extract maximum value from minimum reading, and build knowledge that compounds. So define the question tightly, time-box your research phases, study the most insightful 10% in depth rather than covering 100% superficially, triangulate important facts, read intros and conclusions first, and write notes with context and source so they still mean something a year later. The digging stops at the plateau of diminishing returns: "Once I meet my criterion, I allow myself to stop digging."

Adding an `archived_at` column "seems to ooze complexity out into queries, operations, and applications" — indexes, migrations, and restore code all have to work around dead data, and restoring a record is rarely as simple as `SET archived_at = null`. If the author were starting a new project today, "I'd reach for the trigger-based approach first": a generic archive table fed by a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger, which keeps live tables clean and needs no extra infrastructure. WAL-based CDC and a delete-ignoring replica are weighed as alternatives, but "significant operational complexity" and risk to primary stability are the tradeoffs.

Using AI agents correctly is a process of *reviewing code*: LLMs are good at producing a lot of code, but "they don't yet have the depth of judgement of a competent software engineer," so left unsupervised they commit to bad design decisions and burn hours of effort. The biggest mistake engineers make in code review is "**only thinking about the code that was written, not the code that *could have been* written**" — the best review is *structural*, bringing in context the diff didn't mention so the diff gets shorter and more elegant, and nitpicky or rubber-stamp reviewers will struggle to steer agents away from architectural dead ends. The dominant programming model is something like "centaur chess": the better you are at assessing whether a particular software approach is sensible, the better you'll be at using agentic AI tooling.

Transactions are fundamental to how SQL databases work: a transaction is "a sequence of actions that we want to perform on a database as a single, atomic operation," where `commit` atomically applies every change and `rollback` leaves the database unaltered. Both Postgres and MySQL give a transaction its own consistent read under `REPEATABLE READ`, but Postgres multi-versions rows with `xmin`/`xmax` (cleaned up by `VACUUM FULL`) while MySQL overwrites rows immediately and reconstructs past versions on-the-fly from an undo log. The four isolation levels — Serializable, Repeatable Read, Read Committed, Read Uncommitted — trade isolation against performance, and on conflicting writes MySQL locks rows (and can deadlock) while Postgres uses predicate locks and optimistic conflict resolution; both will kill a transaction to maintain SERIALIZABLE guarantees, so applications "must account for this outcome, and have retry logic for important transactions."

Real-world React and Next.js teams pushed Core Web Vitals, SSR/CSR trade-offs, and caching schemes in production — Vio cut INP from 380ms to 175ms, DoorDash's CSR-to-SSR migration dropped LCP 65% on the homepage, Preply got INP under 200ms without React Server Components or the App Router, GeekyAnts took Lighthouse scores from ~50 to "health scores reached 90+", and Inngest's App Router rebuild killed the blank loading screen. The distilled advice: use SSR to "make it work" then CSR to "make it fast", remember that "long tasks are the enemy of INP", and pare back global state because "simpler is often better". And above all, profile — "performance bottlenecks are often in unexpected places".
